intro: Money touches almost every choice you make. You earn it at a first job. You decide what to spend and what to save. One day you may borrow for a car, school or a home. This unit is about your own money: how to earn it, plan it, grow it and protect it.

You will read a pay stub and see why the number at the bottom is smaller. You will build a budget and watch compound interest grow a small pile of savings. You will learn what APR and a credit score mean. You will also learn to spot scams and read the fine print before you sign.

By the end, you will be able to plan a month of spending and saving with real math. You will compare the true cost of two deals. You will explain when borrowing helps and when it hurts. These are skills you will use for the rest of your life.
bigQuestion: How can you earn, plan, save, borrow and protect money so that it works for you now and later?

Name the opportunity cost of using savings.

title: Personal Finance

chapters.title: Earning, Budgeting and Saving
chapters.bigQuestion: How can you make the money you earn cover what you need today and still grow for later?

story.title: The Smaller Number
story.kicker: Marcus worked 40 hours and expected one number. The check showed another.
paragraphs: Marcus is fifteen. This summer he got his first job at a snow-cone stand near a Chicago park. The pay was $12 an hour in this example. In two weeks he worked 40 hours. He did the math on the bus: 40 times $12 is $480. He already knew what he would buy.

On Friday his manager handed him an envelope. Inside was a pay stub, a paper that lists what you earned and what was taken out. At the top it said $480. At the bottom, next to the words net pay, it said a smaller number. Marcus stared at it. Had someone made a mistake?

His aunt Rosa looked at the stub with him. She pointed to each line in the middle. One line was Social Security. One was Medicare. One was federal income tax, and one was Illinois income tax. "Nobody made a mistake," she said. "This is the money that pays for roads, schools and help for older people. Everyone who works sees these lines."

Then Rosa asked a question that stuck with him. "Now that you know the real number, what is your plan for it?" Marcus did not have a plan. He had a wish list. By the end of the summer he would learn the difference, and he would watch a small pile of savings start to grow on its own.
story.think: Why do you think the number at the bottom of a pay stub is smaller than the number at the top? Who uses the money that was taken out?

lessons.title: Ways People Earn Income
lessons.mainIdea: Income is money you receive, most often from work, and it comes in several forms.
reading: Think of three workers. Dana earns $15 an hour at a grocery store (an example wage). Luis earns a salary of $52,000 a year. Kim serves food and earns a lower hourly wage plus tips from customers. All three receive *income*, money that comes in.

A *wage* is pay for each hour you work. If Dana works 30 hours, she earns 30 times $15, or $450. A *salary* is a fixed amount for a year, paid in equal parts. Luis is paid every two weeks, 26 times a year, so each check starts at $52,000 divided by 26, or $2,000.

Tips are extra money customers give for good service. Young people also get income from an allowance or small jobs like mowing lawns. Adults may earn interest from savings or money from a business. A common mistake is to think income only means a paycheck. Any money that comes in counts.

words.d: money a person receives, from work, gifts, savings or a business
pay for each hour of work
a set amount of pay for a year of work, paid in equal parts

look.title: Two Summer Jobs
look.text: Job A pays $11 an hour for 20 hours a week. Job B pays a flat $250 a week for the same work. Both are example amounts.
look.prompt: Which job pays more each week? Show your math.

check.q: Dana earns $15 an hour and works 30 hours. What is her pay before anything is taken out?
check.why: Hourly pay times hours: $15 x 30 = $450.

check.q: Which of these is a salary?
choices: $48,000 a year paid in equal parts
check.why: A salary is a fixed yearly amount. The others are a wage, tips and an allowance.

check.q: Luis earns $52,000 a year, paid 26 times a year. How much is each check before taxes?
check.why: $52,000 divided by 26 is $2,000. Dividing by 12 would give a monthly amount, not an every-two-weeks one.

lessons.title: Why Some Jobs Pay More
lessons.mainIdea: Jobs that need rare skills or training, or that few people want to do, usually pay more.
reading: A lifeguard and a nurse both keep people safe. Yet the nurse usually earns more per hour. Why? Wages are a price, the price of work. Like other prices, they depend on how many people can do the job and how many employers want them.

Becoming a nurse takes years of school. Fewer people have that skill, and hospitals need many nurses. Many people can learn lifeguarding in a short course. The skills and knowledge a worker builds are called *human capital*. More human capital usually means higher pay.

Other things matter too. Hard or risky jobs, like work on a high bridge, often pay extra. Jobs in big cities may pay more because living there costs more. A common mistake is to think pay shows how important a job is. It mostly shows how scarce the skill is compared with how many employers want it.

words.d: the skills, knowledge and training a worker has
the place where workers offer their work and employers hire them

look.title: Two Paths
look.text: Jada could start work at 18 at a store. Or she could spend two years training to become an electrician, earning little during training but more after.
look.prompt: What does Jada give up by training? What might she gain later?

check.q: Why do jobs that need long training often pay more?
choices: The government sets every wage by law
Those jobs have more workers than they need
Fewer people have the skills, so employers compete for them
check.why: Pay is a price for work. Scarce skills that employers want earn a higher price.

check.q: Which is an example of building human capital?
check.why: Human capital is skill and knowledge. A class builds skill.

check.q: A job is dangerous and few people want it. What usually happens to its pay?
choices: It goes up to attract workers
It stays the same as every other job
check.why: Employers must pay extra to get enough people to do a hard or risky job.

lessons.title: Reading a Pay Stub
lessons.mainIdea: Gross pay is what you earn; net pay is what is left after taxes and deductions.
reading: Go back to Marcus. His *gross pay* was $480, the full amount he earned. Two lines on his stub are set by federal law. Social Security takes 6.2% of pay, and Medicare takes 1.45%. So 6.2% of $480 is $29.76, and 1.45% of $480 is $6.96.

Two other lines were income taxes. In this example, $15 went to federal income tax and $14 went to Illinois income tax. Money taken out of a paycheck is a *deduction*. Some workers also have deductions for health insurance or retirement savings.

Add the deductions: $29.76 + $6.96 + $15 + $14 = $65.72. Subtract from gross pay: $480 - $65.72 = $414.28. That is his *net pay*, the money that reaches his bank account. The big lesson: plan your spending with net pay, not gross pay.

words.d: the full amount you earn before anything is taken out
the amount you actually receive after taxes and other deductions
money taken out of a paycheck, such as taxes or insurance

look.title: Marcus's Pay Stub (example)
look.cite: Example pay stub; Social Security 6.2% and Medicare 1.45% are the employee tax rates set by federal law
look.prompt: What share of Marcus's gross pay did he take home? Round to the nearest whole percent.

check.q: Gross pay is $500 and deductions total $70. What is net pay?
check.why: Net pay = gross pay minus deductions: $500 - $70 = $430.

check.q: Social Security takes 6.2% of pay. How much is taken from $200?
Which number should you use to plan a budget?
choices: The largest number on the stub
check.why: Net pay is the money you really have to spend or save.

lessons.title: Needs, Wants and Trade-Offs
lessons.mainIdea: Every dollar can be spent only once, so a budget means choosing among needs and wants.
reading: Marcus has $414 from his check. He wants new sneakers for $120, a game for $60 and concert tickets for $90. He also must pay $40 a month for his phone and give $50 toward bus fare. These are example prices.

A *need* is something you must have to live or work, like food, housing, or a way to get to your job. A *want* is something nice to have but not required. Marcus's bus fare is a need because he rides the bus to work. The concert is a want.

Money is scarce, so each choice has an *opportunity cost*, the next-best thing you give up. If Marcus buys the sneakers, he may give up the concert. A common mistake is to call something a need just because you want it badly. Another is to list every item you skipped as the opportunity cost. It is only the next-best one.

words.d: something required to live or to work, like food, housing or transportation
something nice to have but not required
the next-best thing you give up when you make a choice

look.title: Marcus's List
look.text: After his phone and bus fare, Marcus has $324 left. The sneakers cost $120, the game $60 and the concert $90 (example prices). He also wants to save something.
look.prompt: If he buys all three, how much is left to save? Which one would you drop, and what is its opportunity cost?

check.q: Which is a need for a worker who rides the bus to work?
check.why: The bus gets the worker to the job, so fare is required.

check.q: Marcus picks sneakers over the concert. His next-best choice was the concert. What is his opportunity cost?
choices: The concert and the game and savings
check.why: Opportunity cost is only the next-best thing given up, not the item chosen or a list.

check.q: Marcus has $324. He buys items costing $120, $60 and $90. How much is left?

lessons.title: Building a Monthly Budget
lessons.mainIdea: A budget is a plan that lists income, then spending and saving, so money in covers money out.
reading: A *budget* is a plan for your money. Start with income. Then list what you expect to spend and save. The two sides should match. Let us build one for Ana, a young adult with $2,000 a month in net pay (an example).

Ana plans: rent $800, food $300, bus pass $75, phone $50, fun $250, clothes $125 and savings $400. Add them: $800 + $300 + $75 + $50 + $250 + $125 + $400 = $2,000. Every dollar has a job. Some expenses are fixed, the same each month, like rent. Others are variable, like food, which changes.

A budget works only if you track what really happens. Ana writes down what she spends for a month. She finds she spent $380 on food, not $300. So she cuts fun to $170 to stay even. If spending is more than income, a person runs short and may have to borrow.

words.d: a plan that shows expected income, spending and saving
a cost that stays the same each month, like rent
a cost that changes from month to month, like food

look.title: Ana's Monthly Budget (example)
look.cite: Made-up example budget for a $2,000 monthly net income
look.prompt: Which items are fixed expenses? What share of Ana's income goes to savings?

check.q: Ana spends $80 more on food than planned. What is one way to keep her budget balanced?
choices: Spend $80 less on something else, like fun
check.why: A budget balances when spending changes in one line are offset in another.

check.q: Which is a variable expense?
check.why: Grocery costs change each month. The others stay the same.

check.q: Income is $1,500. Planned spending and saving total $1,650. What is the problem?
choices: Planned spending is $150 more than income
check.why: $1,650 - $1,500 = $150 over. The plan spends money that is not there.

lessons.title: The 50/30/20 Idea
lessons.mainIdea: One simple guide splits net income into 50% needs, 30% wants and 20% savings.
reading: There is no single right budget. One popular guide is called 50/30/20. It is just one example of a starting point. It says about 50% of net income goes to needs, 30% to wants and 20% to savings or paying off debt.

Try it with $2,000 a month. 50% of $2,000 is $1,000 for needs. 30% is $600 for wants. 20% is $400 for savings. Check: $1,000 + $600 + $400 = $2,000. Try $1,200: $600 needs, $360 wants and $240 savings.

The guide may not fit everyone. In a city where rent is high, needs may take 60% or more. Then wants must shrink to keep savings. A common mistake is to treat 50/30/20 as a law. It is a tool to help you think about balance.

words.d: money set aside now to use later
the money you actually receive after taxes and deductions

look.title: Testing the Guide
look.text: Jordan's net pay is $3,000 a month. Rent, food, transport and insurance cost $1,800 (example amounts).
look.prompt: Using 50/30/20, how much should go to needs? Is Jordan above or below? What would you change?

check.q: Using 50/30/20, how much of $2,500 goes to savings?
Using 50/30/20, how much of $1,800 goes to wants?
A person's needs take 60% of income. To keep saving 20%, what must happen?
check.why: The parts must add to 100%: 60 + 20 + 20 = 100.

lessons.title: Saving Goals and Emergency Funds
lessons.mainIdea: Saving works best with a clear goal, and an emergency fund protects you from surprise costs.
reading: Tasha wants a $600 laptop. She can save $50 a week from her job. $600 divided by $50 is 12, so she will reach her goal in 12 weeks. A *saving goal* names what you want, how much it costs and when you want it.

Now picture a surprise. Tasha's bike breaks, and the repair costs $150. Without savings, she might borrow and pay extra. An *emergency fund* is money kept only for surprises like repairs, medical bills or losing a job. Many advisers suggest adults keep three to six months of expenses in one.

Savings goals can be short term, like a laptop in a few months. They can be long term, like college or a home years away. One helpful habit is to pay yourself first. Move savings out as soon as you are paid, before spending on wants.

words.d: money saved only for unexpected costs, like repairs or losing a job
a plan that names what you are saving for, how much and by when

look.title: Pay Yourself First
look.text: Leo earns $400 a month (example). He usually saves whatever is left at the end of the month, which is often nothing.
look.prompt: If Leo moves $60 into savings on payday, how much will he save in a year? Why might this work better?

check.q: A bike costs $300. You save $25 a week. How many weeks until you can buy it?
check.why: $300 divided by $25 = 12 weeks.

check.q: What is an emergency fund for?
choices: Surprise costs, like a car repair
check.why: An emergency fund covers costs you did not expect.

check.q: An adult's expenses are $2,000 a month. What would a three-month emergency fund hold?

lessons.title: Simple and Compound Interest
lessons.mainIdea: Simple interest is paid only on the starting amount; compound interest is also paid on interest already earned.
reading: When you keep money in a bank savings account, the bank pays you *interest*. Interest is a payment for letting someone use your money. The starting amount is called the *principal*. Say you put $100 in an account that pays 5% a year (an example rate).

With *simple interest*, you earn 5% of the $100, or $5, each year. After 3 years you have $100 + $5 + $5 + $5 = $115. The formula is principal times rate times years: $100 x 0.05 x 3 = $15 of interest.

With *compound interest*, you earn interest on your interest too. Year 1: $100 x 1.05 = $105. Year 2: $105 x 1.05 = $110.25. Year 3: $110.25 x 1.05 = $115.76. That is 76 cents more than simple interest. The gap is small at first, but it grows larger every year.

words.d: money paid for the use of money; savers earn it and borrowers pay it
the starting amount of money saved or borrowed
interest paid only on the principal
interest paid on the principal and on interest already earned

look.title: $100 at 5% a Year, Compounded (example)
look.cite: Made-up example: $100 at an example 5% yearly rate, compounded once a year
look.prompt: How much did the account grow in the first year? About how much in ten years?

check.q: You save $200 at 3% simple interest for 2 years. How much interest do you earn?
check.why: Simple interest = $200 x 0.03 x 2 = $12. $212 is the total, not the interest.

check.q: $100 earns 10% compound interest a year. How much is in the account after 2 years?
check.why: Year 1: $110. Year 2: $110 x 1.10 = $121. $120 would be simple interest.

check.q: Why does compound interest grow faster than simple interest?
choices: The bank adds a bonus every week
You earn interest on past interest
check.why: Each year's interest is added to the balance, so the next year's interest is figured on a bigger amount.

lessons.title: Why Starting Early Matters
lessons.mainIdea: Because of compounding, money saved early has more years to grow than money saved later.
reading: Meet two savers. Each uses an account paying 6% a year, an example rate. Maya puts in $1,000 at age 16. Sam waits and puts in $1,000 at age 28. Neither adds more money. Who ends up with more?

A shortcut called the *Rule of 72* estimates how long money takes to double. Divide 72 by the interest rate. 72 divided by 6 is 12, so money at 6% doubles about every 12 years. By age 28, Maya's $1,000 has become about $2,000, just as Sam starts.

By age 40, Sam's money has doubled once, to about $2,000. Maya's has doubled twice, to about $4,000. She saved the same amount, but she gave it more time. The key is time, not a big first deposit. A common mistake is to think small savings do not matter. Small amounts saved early can grow a lot.

words.d: interest paid on the principal and on interest already earned
a shortcut: divide 72 by the yearly interest rate to estimate the years it takes money to double

look.title: Two Savers
look.text: Maya saves $1,000 at 16. Sam saves $1,000 at 28. Both earn an example 6% a year and add nothing more.
look.prompt: Use the Rule of 72. How much does each have at 52? What did Maya's early start earn her?

check.q: Using the Rule of 72, about how long does money take to double at 8% a year?
check.why: 72 divided by 8 = 9 years.

check.q: Money doubles every 12 years. $500 is saved at 20. About how much is there at 44?
check.why: From 20 to 44 is 24 years, or two doublings: $500 to $1,000 to $2,000.

check.q: Why did Maya end with more than Sam, though both saved $1,000?
choices: Her money had more years to compound
check.why: Same amount, same rate. The only difference was time.

lessons.title: Where to Keep Your Savings
lessons.mainIdea: Banks and credit unions keep savings safe, and federal insurance protects deposits up to $250,000.
reading: Keeping cash in a shoe box earns no interest, and it can be lost or stolen. A *savings account* at a bank or credit union keeps money safe and pays interest. A *credit union* is a bank-like group owned by its members.

If a bank fails, deposits are protected. The FDIC insures bank deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, for each type of account. Credit unions have similar protection from a federal agency called the NCUA. So Marcus's $300 in savings is safe even if his bank has trouble.

Banks offer choices. A savings account lets you take money out easily. A *certificate of deposit*, or CD, often pays a higher rate. The catch is that you agree to leave the money there for a set time. The trade-off is easy access versus higher interest.

words.d: a bank account that keeps money safe and pays interest
a bank-like institution owned by its members
a deposit you leave in a bank for a set time, often for a higher interest rate

look.title: Adam Smith on Saving
look.text: Capitals are increased by parsimony, and diminished by prodigality and misconduct.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, Book II, Chapter 3, 1776
look.prompt: Parsimony means careful saving. Prodigality means wasteful spending. Put Smith's sentence into your own words.

check.q: What does FDIC insurance do?
choices: Protects bank deposits up to $250,000 if a bank fails
check.why: The FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, for each account type.

check.q: Why might someone choose a CD over a savings account?
choices: It often pays a higher rate
They can take money out any day with no penalty
check.why: CDs often pay more in exchange for leaving the money for a set time.

check.q: What is a downside of keeping savings in cash at home?
choices: It earns no interest and can be lost
It grows faster than a bank account
check.why: Cash at home does not grow and has no insurance.

review.q: Gross pay is $600. Deductions total $90. What is net pay?
You save $400 at 5% simple interest for 3 years. How much interest do you earn?

choices: A second pair of name-brand shoes
review.why: You can live and work without extra designer shoes.

review.q: Using 50/30/20, how much of $3,000 goes to needs?
$200 earns 10% compound interest a year. How much after 2 years?
Which pays you a set amount for a year of work?
review.why: A salary is a fixed yearly amount; a wage is paid per hour.

review.q: Why do many advisers suggest an emergency fund?
choices: To pay surprise costs without borrowing
To earn the highest possible return
review.why: An emergency fund is for the unexpected, so you do not need to borrow.

review.q: At 6% a year, about how long does it take money to double?

chapters.title: Credit, Borrowing and Protecting Your Money
chapters.bigQuestion: When does borrowing help you, and how can you keep your money safe from high costs and scams?

story.title: Zero Down, Read the Rest
story.kicker: The sign said $0 down. The fine print told a longer story.
paragraphs: Priya walked past a phone store on State Street in Chicago. A bright sign in the window said NEW PHONE, $0 DOWN! Her old phone had a cracked screen. The new one cost $999 in this example. She did not have $999, but $0 sounded perfect.

Inside, a salesperson smiled and slid a tablet across the counter. "Just sign here," he said. "It is only $35 a month." Priya's older cousin Dev was with her. He asked a simple question. "For how many months?"

The answer was on the second page, in small letters. It said 36 months. There was also a $15 activation fee, and she had to keep a $70-a-month phone plan. Dev took out his calculator. $35 times 36 months is $1,260. That was $261 more than the $999 price.

Priya did not sign that day. She went home and made a list of questions. What is the total cost? What happens if I miss a payment? What if I want to leave early? The sign was not a lie, but it was not the whole story. That is why people read the fine print.
story.think: Why would a store advertise $0 down instead of the total price? What questions should you ask before signing?

lessons.title: Credit: Buy Now, Pay Later
lessons.mainIdea: Credit lets you use money now and pay it back later, usually with interest.
reading: *Credit* means borrowing money now and paying it back later. The person or business that lends is the *lender*. The borrower pays back the money borrowed, called the principal. Most lenders also charge interest, the price of using their money.

Here is an example. Jamal borrows $500 from a bank to fix his car so he can get to work. He agrees to pay 10% interest for one year. At the end of the year he owes $500 + $50 = $550. The $50 is the cost of getting the money early.

Credit can help. It lets people buy a home, pay for school or handle a real emergency. It can also hurt. Borrowing for wants can leave you paying for things long after you enjoy them. A common mistake is to think borrowed money is free. It always costs more than paying cash.

words.d: an agreement to get money, goods or services now and pay later
a person or business that lends money
a person who receives a loan and must pay it back

look.title: Worth Borrowing?
look.text: Case 1: Kira borrows to buy a used car so she can get to a better-paying job. Case 2: Tom borrows to buy a big TV for a party.
look.prompt: Which loan is more likely to pay off in the long run? Explain using costs and benefits.

check.q: Jamal borrows $500 at 10% simple interest for one year. How much does he pay back?
What is interest from a borrower's view?
choices: A tax paid to the city
The price paid for using someone else's money
check.why: Borrowers pay interest as the cost of the loan.

check.q: Which is the best reason to borrow?
choices: To pay for training that raises future pay
To buy concert tickets you want
To buy a new phone when yours works fine
check.why: Borrowing makes more sense when it helps you earn more later.

lessons.title: Debit Cards and Credit Cards
lessons.mainIdea: A debit card spends your own money; a credit card spends borrowed money that you must repay.
reading: Two cards can look almost the same. A *debit card* takes money straight out of your bank account. If you have $80 in the account and buy a $30 shirt, $50 is left. You cannot easily spend money you do not have.

A *credit card* is different. Each purchase is a small loan from the card company. At the end of the month you get a bill. If you pay the whole balance by the due date, many cards charge no interest. If you pay only part, interest is added to the rest.

Both cards have benefits. Paying on time with a credit card can build a credit history. Credit cards often have strong fraud protection. The danger is that it is easy to spend more than you earn. A common mistake is to think the minimum payment is all you owe.

words.d: a card that takes money directly from your bank account
a card that lets you borrow money for purchases and pay it back later
the amount of money owed on a card or held in an account

look.title: Same Shirt, Two Cards
look.text: Ella buys a $40 shirt with a debit card. Omar buys the same shirt with a credit card and pays only $10 when the bill comes.
look.prompt: Where did each person's money come from? What happens to Omar's remaining $30?

check.q: You have $120 in your bank account and spend $45 with a debit card. What is left?
check.why: $120 - $45 = $75. Debit takes money right from your account.

check.q: How can you avoid paying interest on most credit cards?
choices: Pay the full balance by the due date
check.why: Many cards charge no interest if the full balance is paid on time.

check.q: Which is true of a credit card?
choices: It spends only money already in your account
It is the same as cash
Each purchase is borrowed money you must repay
check.why: A credit card is a loan. A debit card uses your own money.

lessons.title: APR in Plain Words
lessons.mainIdea: APR is the yearly cost of borrowing shown as a percent, and a higher APR means a more expensive loan.
reading: Loans and credit cards list an *APR*, or annual percentage rate. It is the cost of borrowing for a year, shown as a percent. It can include some fees as well as interest. Comparing APRs is a quick way to see which loan costs less.

Say a credit card has an APR of 24%, an example rate. Divide by 12 months: 24 divided by 12 is 2% a month. If you carry a $1,000 balance, one month of interest is about 2% of $1,000, or $20. Leave it for a year and it adds up to hundreds of dollars.

Now compare two offers for a $1,000 loan for one year. Offer A has an APR of 8%. Offer B has an APR of 20%. Using simple yearly interest, A costs about $80 and B costs about $200. A lower monthly payment can hide a higher APR or a longer loan. Look at both.

words.d: annual percentage rate; the yearly cost of borrowing, shown as a percent
the smallest amount you must pay on a bill each month to avoid a late fee

look.title: Interest on a $1,000 Balance for One Year (example)
look.cite: Made-up example using simple yearly interest on a $1,000 balance
look.prompt: How much more does the 24% APR cost than the 8% APR?

check.q: A card has an APR of 18%. About what is the monthly rate?
check.why: 18% divided by 12 months = 1.5% a month.

check.q: Which $2,000 loan for one year costs less?
check.why: The lower APR means less interest: 9% of $2,000 is $180.

check.q: A $600 balance on a card with 2% monthly interest is left for one month. About how much interest is added?

lessons.title: What a Credit Score Is
lessons.mainIdea: A credit score is a number that shows lenders how likely you are to repay on time.
reading: Lenders want to know if you will pay them back. So they check your *credit report*. It is a record of your loans and cards and whether you paid on time. Companies called credit bureaus collect this record. You have the right to see your own reports for free.

A *credit score* turns that record into one number. The most widely used scores run from 300 to 850. A higher score tells lenders you are lower risk. People with higher scores often get loans at lower interest rates.

Here is why that matters. Two people borrow $20,000 for a car. One gets an example rate of 5% because of a strong score. The other gets 12%. In the first year alone, that is about $1,000 versus about $2,400 in interest. A good score can save real money.

words.d: a record of a person's borrowing and whether bills were paid on time
a number, often from 300 to 850, that shows how likely a person is to repay debts

look.title: Two Borrowers
look.text: Ben pays every bill on time. Carla has missed several payments. Both ask for the same $10,000 loan.
look.prompt: Which person is likely to get the lower interest rate? Why does the lender care?

check.q: What does a higher credit score usually mean for a borrower?
check.why: Lenders see lower risk, so they charge less.

check.q: What range do the most widely used credit scores cover?
check.why: The most common scores run from 300 to 850.

check.q: A $20,000 loan at 5% versus 12% for one year. About how much more interest at 12%?

lessons.title: What Changes Your Score
lessons.mainIdea: Paying on time and keeping balances low are the biggest ways to build a good credit score.
reading: The company FICO makes the most widely used score. It publishes the rough weight of each part. Payment history, whether you pay on time, counts most, about 35%. How much you owe counts about 30%.

Length of credit history counts about 15%. New credit, meaning recent loan applications, counts about 10%. Credit mix, the kinds of credit you have, counts about 10%. Add them: 35 + 30 + 15 + 10 + 10 = 100.

So the best habits are simple. Pay every bill on time. Keep card balances well below the limit. Say your limit is $1,000 and you owe $900. You are using 90% of your credit, which can lower your score. Owing $200 uses only 20%. A common myth is that checking your own report hurts your score. It does not.

words.d: the record of how long and how well a person has handled credit
the most a lender lets you borrow on a card

look.title: What Goes Into a FICO Score
look.cite: myFICO (Fair Isaac Corporation), "What's in my FICO Scores?" general weights
look.prompt: Which two parts together make up about two-thirds of the score?

check.q: Which habit helps a credit score the most?
choices: Opening many new cards at once
Using all of your credit limit
check.why: Payment history is the largest part, about 35%.

check.q: Your limit is $2,000 and you owe $500. What percent of your credit are you using?
Does checking your own credit report lower your score?
check.why: Looking at your own report does not hurt your score.

lessons.title: Loans for Big Things
lessons.mainIdea: Big purchases like cars, college and homes often use loans that are repaid in monthly payments over years.
reading: Some things cost too much to pay for all at once. Many people use a *loan* repaid in set monthly payments. Three common kinds are car loans, student loans and mortgages. Each one works a little differently.

A car loan usually lasts a few years. A *student loan* pays for college or training. Payments often start after school ends. A *mortgage* is a loan to buy a home, often over 15 or 30 years. If the borrower stops paying, the lender can take the car or the home. That property is called *collateral*.

Longer loans have smaller payments but cost more in total. Say a loan has payments of $300 a month for 48 months (an example). The total is $300 x 48 = $14,400. Another choice is $250 a month for 72 months. That total is $250 x 72 = $18,000. The lower payment costs $3,600 more.

words.d: money borrowed that must be repaid, usually with interest
a loan used to buy a home, repaid over many years
a loan that pays for college or job training
property a lender can take if a loan is not repaid

look.title: Longer or Shorter?
look.text: Two car loans for the same car: $400 a month for 36 months, or $300 a month for 60 months (example amounts).
look.prompt: Find the total cost of each. Which would you choose, and what is the trade-off?

check.q: A loan is $400 a month for 36 months. What is the total paid?
What is a mortgage?
choices: A loan to buy a home
check.why: A mortgage is a home loan, often lasting 15 or 30 years.

check.q: Why does a longer loan with smaller payments often cost more in total?
choices: The price of the item rises
The bank adds a free month
You pay interest for more months
check.why: More time borrowing means more interest paid in total.

lessons.title: Spotting Scams and Phishing
lessons.mainIdea: Scammers create pressure and ask for private information, so slow down and check before you act.
reading: Mia gets a text: "Your bank account is locked! Click here and enter your password now." It looks real. But it is a *scam*, a trick to steal money or information. This kind, where a fake message fishes for private details, is called *phishing*.

Scams often share warning signs. They rush you: act now or lose out. They ask for passwords, account numbers or a Social Security number. They ask you to pay with gift cards or a money app. They promise prizes you never entered to win.

What helps: stop and do not click. Contact the company yourself using a number or website you already trust. Real banks do not ask for your password by text. Tell a trusted adult. You can report scams to the Federal Trade Commission, the U.S. agency that protects consumers.

words.d: a trick to steal someone's money or personal information
a fake email, text or call that tries to get private information

look.title: Is It Real?

look.prompt: List every warning sign you can find. What should you do?

check.q: Which is a warning sign of a scam?
choices: A demand to pay right away with gift cards
A receipt from a store where you shopped
A bill for a service you used
A letter you expected from school
check.why: Pressure plus gift-card payment is a common scam sign.

check.q: A text says your bank account is locked and asks for your password. What should you do?
choices: Contact the bank yourself using a number you trust
check.why: Real banks do not ask for passwords by text. Check through a trusted channel.

check.q: What is phishing?
choices: A safe way to pay bills
A fake message that tries to get private information
check.why: Phishing fishes for passwords and account numbers with fake messages.

lessons.title: Guarding Against Identity Theft
lessons.mainIdea: Identity theft is when someone uses your personal information, and simple habits make it much harder.
reading: *Identity theft* happens when someone uses your name, Social Security number or account numbers without permission. A thief might open a credit card in your name. Then you learn about it when the bills or a low credit score show up.

Simple habits help. Use strong, different passwords for important accounts. Turn on two-step login when you can. Do not share your Social Security number unless it is truly needed. Shred papers with account numbers before throwing them away.

Check your bank statements and credit reports. You can get free credit reports from the three national credit bureaus through AnnualCreditReport.com. If something looks wrong, act fast. The FTC's IdentityTheft.gov site gives step-by-step recovery plans. Catching a problem early limits the damage.

words.d: using someone else's personal information without permission, often to steal money
details like your Social Security number, passwords and account numbers

look.title: Something Looks Wrong

look.prompt: What steps should Leah take, and in what order?

check.q: Which habit best protects against identity theft?
choices: Posting your birthday and address online
Throwing old bank papers in the trash whole
check.why: Different strong passwords mean one leak does not open every account.

check.q: How can you get free credit reports from the national bureaus?
check.why: AnnualCreditReport.com is the official site for free reports.

check.q: Why check your bank statement each month?
choices: To catch charges you did not make
check.why: Finding strange charges early limits the damage.

lessons.title: What Insurance Is For
lessons.mainIdea: Insurance lets many people pay small amounts so that no one has to face a huge loss alone.
reading: Imagine 1,000 drivers. Each year, a few of them will have a costly accident. No one knows who. *Insurance* is a deal: each person pays a small, regular amount, called a *premium*. The company uses the pool of money to pay for the few big losses.

Here is an example. Each driver pays $1,200 a year. That is $1.2 million from all 1,000 drivers. If 20 drivers each have a $40,000 accident, claims total $800,000. The pool covers them, plus the company's costs. A *deductible* is the part of a loss you pay yourself before insurance pays. Say it is $500 and the repair costs $3,000. You pay $500 and insurance pays $2,500.

Common kinds are health, car, home or renters, and life insurance. Most states, including Illinois, require car insurance to drive. The trade-off is clear. You pay a sure small cost to avoid a possible large one.

words.d: a plan where people pay regular amounts so a company will cover large losses
the regular amount paid for insurance
the part of a loss you pay yourself before insurance pays the rest

look.title: Renters Insurance
look.text: Sam rents an apartment. Renters insurance costs $15 a month (example). His laptop, bike and clothes are worth about $4,000.
look.prompt: What does Sam pay in a year? Is the trade-off worth it? Why or why not?

check.q: A repair costs $2,000. The deductible is $500. How much does insurance pay?
check.why: Insurance pays the loss minus the deductible: $2,000 - $500 = $1,500.

check.q: What is a premium?
choices: The amount insurance pays after a loss
check.why: You pay the premium to keep the insurance.

check.q: Why does insurance work?
choices: Many people's small payments cover a few people's large losses
check.why: Pooling spreads the risk among many people.

lessons.title: Comparing Prices
lessons.mainIdea: Compare the unit price and the total cost, not just the sticker price or the monthly payment.
reading: At the store, a 12-ounce cereal box costs $3.60 and a 20-ounce box costs $5.00. These are example prices. Which is the better deal? Find the *unit price*, the cost for one unit. $3.60 divided by 12 is $0.30 an ounce. $5.00 divided by 20 is $0.25 an ounce. The bigger box costs less per ounce.
The same idea works for bigger buys. Go back to Priya's phone. Paying $999 at once is cheaper than $35 a month for 36 months, which is $1,260. The *total cost* includes every payment and every fee.

A bigger box is only a better deal if you will use it before it spoils. A sale is only a savings if you meant to buy the item anyway. Comparing prices is about value for you, not just the lowest number.

words.d: the cost for one unit, such as one ounce or one item
the full amount paid, including all payments, interest and fees

look.title: Cereal Unit Prices (example)
look.prompt: Which box has the lowest unit price? Why might someone still buy another box?

check.q: A 10-ounce bag costs $2.50. What is the unit price?
check.why: $2.50 divided by 10 ounces = $0.25 an ounce.

check.q: A phone is $50 a month for 24 months plus a $30 fee. What is the total cost?
Which is the best way to compare two sizes of the same item?
choices: Pick the bigger box every time
check.why: Unit price shows the cost per ounce, so different sizes can be compared fairly.

lessons.title: Reading a Contract
lessons.mainIdea: A contract is a promise that the law can enforce, so read it and ask questions before you sign.
reading: A *contract* is an agreement between two or more people that the law can enforce. A phone plan, a loan or an apartment lease is a contract. Once you sign, you usually must do what it says, even if you did not read it.

Look for the key terms. What is the total cost? How long does it last? What fees are there, such as late fees or fees to cancel early? Priya's phone deal had a $15 activation fee and a 36-month term. The *fine print* is the small text where these details often hide.

Before you sign, slow down. Take the papers home if you can. Ask what each fee is for. If a salesperson rushes you, that is a warning sign. In most states, anyone under 18 usually needs a parent or guardian to co-sign a big contract. Never sign a blank or unfinished form.

words.d: an agreement that the law can enforce
the small-print details in a contract, often about fees and rules
how long a contract or loan lasts

check.why: Pressure is a warning sign. A good deal can wait for you to read it.

check.q: What is a contract?
choices: An agreement the law can enforce
check.why: Signing a contract creates legal duties.
